render.title: Proton gradient formation by Complex I
render.summary: Complex I couples NADH oxidation to proton pumping via a long hydrophobic arm. Four protons are translocated per NADH.
render.body:
Complex I (also called NADH dehydrogenase) is an L-shaped protein with two main parts: a hydrophilic arm that sticks into the matrix and a long hydrophobic arm that runs along the inner mitochondrial membrane.

Here is what happens step by step when NADH arrives:

1. NADH binds at the tip of the hydrophilic arm and donates two electrons. This oxidises NADH back to NAD+.

2. The electrons travel along a chain of iron-sulfur clusters down the hydrophilic arm toward the junction with the hydrophobic arm.

3. At the junction, the electrons reduce ubiquinone (coenzyme Q) to ubiquinol. This reduction is the energy-releasing step.

4. The energy released by the reduction drives a series of conformational changes in the hydrophobic arm. The arm contains several membrane-spanning subunits (called ND2, ND4, and ND5 in humans) that each act like a piston or antiporter.

5. These conformational changes physically push four protons from the matrix side across the inner membrane into the intermembrane space. No single channel carries all four; instead each subunit in the arm translocates one or two protons by changing shape.

6. The result is that for every NADH oxidised, four protons are pumped out, adding to the proton gradient that will later drive ATP synthase.

A useful way to picture it: the hydrophilic arm is like the handle of a pump, and the long hydrophobic arm is the pump barrel lying flat in the membrane. Electrons arriving at the handle trigger mechanical strokes down the barrel that push protons across.
